text: Multiple regression gets more flexible with every feature you add. Give it enough features and enough freedom, and it will find patterns that aren't really there — the overfitting you met in Chapter 1. Regularization fights that by adding a penalty to the loss for having large coefficients, so the model has to earn every bit of complexity it uses.

Regularized regression minimizes squared errors plus alpha times a penalty on the coefficients. Ridge uses the sum of squared coefficients — it shrinks all of them toward zero but rarely makes any exactly zero. Lasso uses the sum of absolute values — it can push some coefficients to exactly zero, removing those features entirely, making lasso an embedded feature selector.

Alpha sets the strength — at alpha zero you recover ordinary least squares, and larger values mean more shrinkage and a simpler model. Generating 120 rows with 40 features where only 4 truly matter, then training on just 60 rows, so the model has almost as many coefficients as it has examples — a problem built to overfit.

Comparing OLS, ridge, and lasso: plain OLS scores 0.919 on its own training rows but negative 0.645 on test rows — worse than just predicting the average every time. Ridge gives up some training fit and recovers a test R-squared of 0.492.

Lasso does best here, 0.636 on test, and keeps only 10 of the 40 features. Lower training scores paired with higher test scores is exactly what regularization is for — it's a direct demonstration of trading bias for a better generalization.

Plotting the actual coefficients makes the difference vivid. OLS shows large coefficients in both directions, most of them fitting pure noise. Ridge squeezes every single one toward zero. Lasso leaves most of them at exactly zero and keeps only a handful alive.

Four practical rules. Scale features first — the penalty punishes coefficient size, and size depends on units, so StandardScaler inside a pipeline puts every feature on equal footing. Choose alpha with cross-validation, not by peeking at the test set — RidgeCV and LassoCV do this automatically. Here, LassoCV chose an alpha of about 4.58, scoring 0.638 on test and keeping 11 features.

Pick by goal — ridge suits many small, correlated effects and handles the multicollinearity trap from last lesson more gracefully than plain OLS. Lasso suits a suspicion that only a few features matter, or a need for a sparse, explainable model. ElasticNet blends both penalties together.

And remember, regularization does not create signal — if the data has no real pattern, no penalty will invent one. To recap: ridge shrinks, lasso shrinks and selects. Scale your features, tune alpha by cross-validation, and judge the result on held-out data. Next, we need proper ways to measure how good a regression model actually is: regression metrics.
